newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia urged to set up commodity futures trade.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia urged to set up commodity futures trade.

text.p: Indonesia's plan to establish a commodity futures exchange should not be derailed by recent high-profile scandals on world financial markets, an economist told a parliamentary panel on Wednesday.

Christianto Wibisono told the commission Jakarta should not be deterred by the huge losses in unauthorised derivatives trades that sank the British bank Barings in 1995 or $2.6 billion in losses in unauthorised copper trading incurred by a Sumitomo Corp trader over a 10-year period.
"We cannot be too afraid or worried over the risks looking at the Baring and Sumitomo cases as they are the exception," said Wibisono, director of the private Indonesian Business Data Centre.
The panel is hearing opinions from various sources on the government proposal to set up a futures exchange that would initially trade in crude palm oil and coffee.
The government has not said when the exchange, to be run by the private sector under government supervision, would become operational, but industry sources are looking at late 1997.
After neighbouring Malaysia, Indonesia is the world's second-largest producer of crude palm oil, which is used to make cooking oil, cosmetics and toiletries such as soap and shampoo.
Indonesia is also the world's third-largest coffee producer after Brazil and Colombia.
Economist Wibisono said setting up a futures exchange would help producers hedge against price fluctuations while helping buyers ensure steady long-term supply.

"In between these two players, there will be speculators who will take risks, so there will be some gambling in futures trading," he said. "But this has to be understood in the context of risk management...on managing and anticipating risks."

Wibisono said Indonesia should venture into futures trading so as not to fall behind countries. But he added that the government should adopt regulations used in exchanges in Britain and the United States.
Industry sources welcomed the proposal to introduce futures trading but said the exchange should be transparent, liquid and sufficiently regulated to ensure its success.

"It's about time Indonesia set up its own futures exchange," one senior trader said. "Indonesia is the world's second-largest producer of crude palm oil, and Indonesians still depend on the Kuala Lumpur Commodity Exchange to hedge."

"Having said that, the proposed exchange must be liquid, otherwise it can be manipulated by the big boys," he said. "The market must also be transparent, in that all transactions are above board and there are proper rules governing transactions."
Nafis Daulay, chairman of the Indonesian Edible Oils Industry Association, said success would also hinge on the participation of state plantations.
"State plantations produce nearly 50 percent of the country's total output, and therefore should sell their oil through the exchange," he said.

The state-run Joint Marketing Board exports some 30 percent of the crude palm oil produced by government-owned plantations through a Hamburg-based state-owned Indonesian company, Indoham. The rest is sold domestically.
Daulay said the government also needed to clarify the role of state logistics agency BULOG, which regulates the commodity market, after the exchange is established.
BULOG intervenes in the market when it feels local cooking oil prices are too high by importing crude palm oil-based cooking oil or palm olein and selling it below market prices.
